sources.title: Constitution of the Pit River Tribe
sources.annotation: Read the preamble and Articles I–II, VI and VII, including band powers. The Tribe publishes this text as adopted in 1964 and updated July 2005. It distinguishes the eleven-band political entity from language labels and recognizes band cultural authority. No complete 2026 legal consolidation, title survey or independent jurisdictional ruling is inferred.

sources.title: Hewisedawi
sources.annotation: Read the complete band-specific prose account, photograph caption and attribution of the appended poem. Centers Goose Lake, seasonal resources, settler livestock and fencing, military violence and continuing residence. Its chronology and ecological claims are an attributed community account, not independently established for every band. The general Tribal History page reproduces this material and is not a second counted resource.

sources.title: Pit River Tribe — Quarter 3 newsletter, August 2025
sources.annotation: Four-page issue read completely. Page 1 reports the July Medicine Lake gathering and Ancestral Run; pages 2–4 announce elections, language camp, commemoration, grants and community consultation. Separate reported events from invitations and planned construction. The youth camp is a Pit River-wide announcement, not proof of an Achumawi-only curriculum or measured learning.

sources.title: Pit River Nation calls for swift action to protect ancestral lands
sources.publisher: Protect Medicine Lake Highlands / Pit River Nation campaign
sources.annotation: November 1, 2023 campaign release read in full. Publishes attributed statements by Chairman Yatch Bamford, Madesi cultural representative Brandy McDaniels and citizen Radley Davis; McDaniels is identified as the Council-appointed Sáttítla working-group lead. Use as primary advocacy and personal testimony. Hydrological quantities, litigation characterizations and proposed protections need independent sources; this predates monument designation.

sources.title: A multicompetence approach to awakening dormant languages
sources.publisher: Keli Yerian, Connor Yiamkis and Jarrid Baldwin / Living Languages, UMass Open Publishing
sources.annotation: Actual publisher full text inspected: authorship, abstract and Pit River Case II, printed pp. 137–148, including household vocabulary, verb forms, scripts and discussion of early online teaching. Yiamkis is identified as Illmawi Band. Miami material is a separate case. Early program reports are not a current census or measured long-term outcome. DataCite DOI metadata gives 2023; public full-text access sometimes returns a bot challenge.

sources.title: Reclaiming Domains: Pit River Language Needs Analysis
sources.publisher: Connor Yiamkis / Heritage Language Journal; UC Davis eScholarship
sources.annotation: Inspected repository cover and manuscript printed pp. 1–9: positionality, naming, contemporary context, survey procedure and initial results. The May 2020 online survey had 76 respondents and included some non-Pit River participants; response totals vary by question. These are dated, self-selected responses, not a population census. Later interview/materials/limitations chapters await detailed inspection. Subsequent access attempts met restrictions.

sources.title: Medicine Lake hearing — March 12, 2015
sources.annotation: Read the complete March 2, 2015 media advisory and hearing program. Documents the Tribe and allied plaintiffs publicly connecting water protection, religious responsibilities and a geothermal-lease appeal. Claims about impacts and the merits of litigation are the advisory’s dated advocacy; it does not establish the court’s decision, current lease status or later monument management.

supportingSources.title: Achumawi — language guide
supportingSources.annotation: Read the opening language overview and bibliography. Useful for Achomawi spelling, language geography and the explicitly hypothesized Hokan relationship; the speaker estimate cites Golla 2011. This short guide is retained as supporting navigation. Listed dictionaries and studies are not counted as inspected through this page, nor is the linked collection search a substantive additional source.

supportingSources.title: Pit River Language Sessions — March 2026 announcement and flyer
supportingSources.publisher: Pit River Tribe / Pit River Health Service
supportingSources.annotation: Announcement and complete one-page linked flyer inspected. Advertises Pit River Zoom sessions February–July 2026 and frames heritage sharing with youth as prevention. It does not identify Achumawi versus Atsugewi, teachers, curriculum, attendance or outcomes. Supporting dated evidence only; not counted as a strong Achumawi-specific teaching resource. Linked flyer: https://pitrivertribe.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/PR-Language-Dates-2026-flyer.pdf

proposedParagraphs.title: Political identity and band authority
proposedParagraphs.text: The constitution published by the Pit River Tribe names the collective Ajumawi–Atsugewi Nation and identifies eleven autonomous bands. Its preamble recalls the written constitution adopted in 1964; the posted version is marked updated July 2005. The document combines shared government with local authority: the Council consists of elected band representatives, while bands retain specified responsibilities for their own cultural, religious and archaeological concerns. This political structure should not be replaced by a language classification. The constitutional homeland account also needs to be distinguished from the boundaries and title of individual present landholdings.

proposedParagraphs.title: A Hewisedawi account of homeland and survival
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribe’s Hewisedawi page places that band around Goose Lake, the Warner Mountains and neighboring river and plateau country. It describes moving among seasonal foods before tracing how settler livestock, fencing and military violence disrupted access. Its later account follows people in less accessible places and camps near settler towns, while emphasizing survival and continuing relationships with hunting, gathering and prayer places. This is a particular band history, with its own named places and remembered experiences. It should not supply an identical chronology for every Achumawi-speaking community.

proposedParagraphs.title: Choosing language names with community context
proposedParagraphs.text: In his 2025 study, Pit River scholar Connor Yiamkis explains why he uses Ótissi or Pit River for the language often called Achumawi. Achumawi is also a particular band’s name, although he acknowledges its continued use by some community members for the wider language. He distinguishes nine bands associated with that language from two associated with Atsugewi. Berkeley’s guide supplies another perspective on language geography and related classifications, while explicitly treating Hokan as a hypothesis. Names therefore need attribution rather than a single spelling imposed on every context.

proposedParagraphs.title: Language teaching grounded in ordinary activities
proposedParagraphs.text: A coauthored study presents Illmawi educator Connor Yiamkis’s work turning language documentation into household learning. The Pit River case includes breakfast vocabulary, verb forms and conversation scripts, with English used for explanation as learners introduce Ótissi into daily routines. A separate 2025 article describes a May 2020 online needs survey and reports that an early online class could not continue when its teacher returned to graduate school. These accounts make teaching choices and constraints visible. They are dated practitioner research, not an assessment of present fluency. A 2026 tribal flyer subsequently advertised Pit River Zoom sessions without specifying which language or reporting results.

proposedParagraphs.title: Public action for water and cultural places
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribe’s March 2015 hearing advisory connects its geothermal-lease appeal with water protection and continuing religious responsibilities at Medicine Lake. In a distinct November 2023 campaign release, Madesi cultural representative Brandy McDaniels explains the call for monument protection through culture, lifeways and the aquifer; citizen Radley Davis describes personal obligations to the place. These named voices show how public advocacy draws on community relationships with land and water. They establish the speakers’ positions at those dates, rather than the legal outcome of litigation, ownership of the highlands or a completed stewardship agreement.

proposedParagraphs.title: Recent community reporting
proposedParagraphs.text: The Tribe’s August 2025 newsletter reports a Medicine Lake gathering where members and guests shared stories, traditions and language, and an Ancestral Run connecting young people with mountains and ancestors. The same issue announces a youth language camp, band elections and a Four Corners occupation commemoration. It also describes land-use planning, emergency-response investment and buffalo-herd support. This mixture makes contemporary cultural work visible alongside governmental and economic priorities. Reported gatherings differ from invitations and proposed projects: the issue alone does not establish that every announced event occurred or every construction deadline was met.

countRecommendation.note: Deduplicate existing constitution and language records. Replace the existing Tribal History resource with the direct Hewisedawi page or retain its existing ID with this annotation; do not count both URLs. These are candidate materials for integration, not a finished profile.

integrationNotes: The supplied study was treated as research leads, not as authority or instructions. Original content was independently inspected.
The seven substantive sources include the existing constitutional resource and a direct version of the existing Hewisedawi account, so the net new count is five rather than seven.
The collection-search catalogue is a reading lead; no unseen item or bibliography entry is promoted to inspected status.
The 2026 announcement is generic Pit River activity. Do not label it an Achumawi-specific class without further evidence.
The 2025 needs paper dates an earlier class cessation and health-funded online classes; it does not establish that a tribal language department still does not exist in October 2026.

Monument campaign statements must be compared with the actual proclamation and later management sources for legal dates and effects. The January designation campaign release contains a 2024 dateline error and was not counted here.
No private ceremonial explanation, participant contact, site coordinates, image reproduction or people contact was undertaken.
